gloss: Measurements taken at a distance and sent back automatically to a receiver.
examples: The spacecraft stopped sending *telemetry* an hour after launch.
Race engineers watch the car's *telemetry* from the pit wall.
You can turn off the app's *telemetry* in the privacy settings.

gloss: A screen that shows a speaker's script so they can read it while facing the camera.
examples: The anchor read the whole story off a *teleprompter*.
Both *teleprompters* failed, so the senator spoke from memory.
He glanced at the *teleprompter* and lost his place.

gloss: A protective cap at the end of a chromosome that gets shorter as cells divide.
examples: *Telomeres* grow shorter as we age.
The study measured *telomere* length in blood cells.
Each *telomere* shields the DNA underneath it.

gloss: A worker hired for a short period, usually through an agency.
examples: They brought in a *temp* to cover the front desk.
Two *temps* handled the holiday rush.
She worked as a *temp* for a year before they hired her full time.
contrast: In speech *temp* is also short for *temperature*, as in "check the temp on the oven."

gloss: Moderation in drinking alcohol, or giving it up completely.
examples: The *temperance* movement helped bring about Prohibition.
She preached *temperance* at every church meeting.
The county's old *temperance* laws still ban Sunday sales.

gloss: A violent storm, or a sudden burst of uproar.
examples: A *tempest* tore the roof off the boathouse.
One careless post set off a *tempest* in the comments.
Sailors have feared these *tempests* for centuries.

gloss: A Japanese dish of seafood or vegetables fried in a light batter.
examples: We ordered shrimp *tempura* to start.
The *tempura* was crisp and not greasy at all.
She makes *tempura* with sparkling water in the batter.

gloss: A habit of behaving in a certain way, or the general direction something moves in.
examples: He has a *tendency* to interrupt when he gets excited.
Prices show a *tendency* to rise in the spring.
Both kids have the same *tendencies*.

ru: молоток для отбивания мяса; размягчитель мяса
gloss: A tool or powder used to make meat softer.
examples: Pound the steak with a *tenderizer* before you cook it.
She keeps a wooden *tenderizer* in the top drawer.
A little *tenderizer* helps with the tougher cuts.
contrast: British English spells it *tenderiser*, with an s.

gloss: Gentle, caring feeling, or soreness in a part of the body when it is pressed.
examples: He spoke to his mother with real *tenderness*.
The doctor checked for *tenderness* around the knee.
There's still some *tenderness* where the bruise was.

gloss: A cone-shaped tent of poles and hides used by Plains Indian peoples.
examples: The museum has a full-size *tepee* set up outside.
Three *tepees* stood at the edge of the camp.
The kids built a *tepee* out of branches and a tarp.
contrast: Also spelled *teepee* and *tipi*; all three are said TEE-pee.

gloss: A unit of computer storage equal to about a thousand gigabytes.
examples: The new drive holds two *terabytes*.
A single *terabyte* isn't much for video work.
We back up about a *terabyte* of data every night.

gloss: A sweet Japanese sauce made with soy sauce, or food grilled in it.
examples: I ordered chicken *teriyaki* with brown rice.
She brushed *teriyaki* on the salmon before broiling it.
The *teriyaki* was a little too sweet for me.

gloss: A small turtle that lives in fresh or slightly salty water.
examples: A *terrapin* was sunning itself on the log.
The bay is home to diamondback *terrapins*.
We found two baby *terrapins* by the pond.

gloss: A pattern of shapes that fit together with no gaps and no overlaps.
examples: The bathroom floor is a *tessellation* of hexagons.
Escher's prints are full of *tessellations*.
We drew a *tessellation* in geometry class.

gloss: A person or device that tests something, or a sample of a product for customers to try.
examples: The studio hired two *testers* for the beta.
Use the *tester* on the counter before you buy the lipstick.
He works as a game *tester* on the night shift.

gloss: The process of checking how something works or whether someone has a condition.
examples: Drug *testing* is required for every driver.
The software goes into *testing* next week.
Free *testing* was set up at the public library.

gloss: The main male sex hormone.
examples: His doctor checked his *testosterone* levels.
*Testosterone* drops slowly as men get older.
The locker room was all noise and *testosterone*.

gloss: A serious disease caused by bacteria entering a wound, which stiffens the muscles.
examples: She got a *tetanus* shot after stepping on a nail.
*Tetanus* is rare here because most children are vaccinated.
The clinic gives *tetanus* boosters every ten years.

gloss: A playground game in which two players hit a ball on a rope around a pole.
examples: We played *tetherball* every recess in fourth grade.
The school put in a new *tetherball* pole.
He is still unbeatable at *tetherball*.

gloss: A solid shape with four triangular faces.
examples: A *tetrahedron* has four faces and four corners.
She folded the paper into a small *tetrahedron*.
The model was built out of plastic *tetrahedrons*.
contrast: Everyday plural is *tetrahedrons*; math writing often uses *tetrahedra*.

gloss: A poetic meter with four beats in each line.
examples: The poem is written in iambic *tetrameter*.
*Tetrameter* moves faster than pentameter.
He switched to *tetrameter* halfway through the sequence.

gloss: A structure deep in the brain that passes signals from the senses to the cortex.
examples: The *thalamus* relays almost everything the senses pick up.
Damage to the *thalamus* can disrupt sleep.
The scan showed swelling near the *thalamus*.
contrast: The plural is *thalami*, said THAL-uh-my.

gloss: Belief in a god, especially one who takes an active part in the world.
examples: The course compares *theism* and atheism.
His argument for *theism* rests on the idea of design.
She moved from *theism* to agnosticism during college.

gloss: A government run by religious leaders or according to religious law.
examples: The revolution turned the country into a *theocracy*.
He warned that the new law was a step toward *theocracy*.
Few *theocracies* last long in the modern world.

gloss: Someone who studies religion and religious belief.
examples: The *theologian* spoke at the divinity school last night.
Two *theologians* debated the passage for an hour.
She's a *theologian* who writes for a general audience.

gloss: A mathematical statement that has been proved to be true.
examples: We proved the *theorem* in class today.
The Pythagorean *theorem* is the one everybody remembers.
His proof of the *theorem* runs two hundred pages.

gloss: Someone who develops ideas that explain how something works.
examples: She's a leading *theorist* of urban planning.
The *theorists* disagree about what caused the collapse.
As a political *theorist*, he writes more than he teaches.

gloss: The layer of the atmosphere above the mesosphere, where temperature rises with height.
examples: The space station orbits inside the *thermosphere*.
Auroras form high up in the *thermosphere*.
The *thermosphere* begins about fifty miles up.

gloss: An object, event, or matter that you do not name more exactly.
examples: What's that *thing* on the top shelf?
A few *things* still bother me about the plan.
The best *thing* about the job is the people.

gloss: A person who thinks deeply, especially one with important ideas.
examples: He was one of the great *thinkers* of his generation.
She's a careful *thinker* and a slow writer.
The book profiles six *thinkers* who changed economics.

gloss: The activity of using your mind, or a person's current view on a question.
examples: The class is meant to teach critical *thinking*.
My *thinking* on this has changed a lot since March.
Wishful *thinking* won't balance the budget.

gloss: Underwear or a sandal with a narrow strip that passes between the legs or toes, or a thin strip of leather.
examples: She wore a *thong* under the thin dress.
The sandal's *thong* snapped on the beach.
He tied the bundle shut with a leather *thong*.
contrast: In Australia *thongs* are flip-flops; in the US the word usually means underwear.

gloss: A horse of pure breeding, especially one bred for racing.
examples: Her grandfather raised *thoroughbreds* in Kentucky.
The *thoroughbred* won by two lengths.
He paid far too much for an untested *thoroughbred*.

gloss: Careful attention to every detail of a job.
examples: The inspector's *thoroughness* impressed everyone.
I admire her *thoroughness*, even when it slows us down.
The report was praised for its *thoroughness*.

gloss: Careful, economical use of money.
examples: Her *thrift* got the family through the recession.
He runs the shop with old-fashioned *thrift*.
*Thrift* stores do good business when money is tight.

gloss: A book, movie, or play with an exciting, suspenseful plot.
examples: I read a legal *thriller* on the flight.
The movie is a slow-burn *thriller* with a great ending.
She writes *thrillers* set in small towns.

gloss: The ceremonial chair of a king or queen, or royal power itself.
examples: The queen sat on a gold *throne*.
He came to the *throne* at nineteen.
Two brothers fought over the *throne* for a decade.
contrast: *Throne* sounds exactly like *thrown*, the past participle of *throw*.

gloss: An act of throwing something, or a light blanket for a couch or chair.
examples: His *throw* to first base sailed wide.
She keeps a wool *throw* over the armchair.
Each player gets three *throws*.

gloss: A songbird with a spotted breast and a musical call.
examples: A *thrush* sang from the hedge at dawn.
*Thrushes* nest in the woods behind the house.
The wood *thrush* is common in the eastern states.

gloss: The mark left by the pattern of lines on the tip of a thumb.
examples: There was a greasy *thumbprint* on the screen.
The phone unlocks with my *thumbprint*.
Police found two clear *thumbprints* on the glass.
contrast: The b is silent: THUM-print.

gloss: A short pin with a wide flat head, pushed in with the thumb to hold paper on a board.
examples: She pinned the map up with four *thumbtacks*.
A *thumbtack* fell out of the corkboard.
Don't leave *thumbtacks* lying on the floor.
contrast: American *thumbtack* is British *drawing pin*; the b is silent.

gloss: A gland in the upper chest where cells of the immune system mature.
examples: The *thymus* shrinks as a person gets older.
T cells finish developing in the *thymus*.
Surgeons removed part of his *thymus*.

gloss: A small repeated movement or sound that a person cannot fully control.
examples: He has a *tic* that makes him blink hard.
Her verbal *tics* show up when she's nervous.
The medication reduced his *tics* within a month.
contrast: *Tic* sounds just like *tick*, the insect or the sound of a clock.

gloss: A running display of stock prices or headlines, or the short code that identifies a stock.
examples: The *ticker* at the bottom of the screen showed the closing prices.
Apple trades under the *ticker* AAPL.
News *tickers* scrolled all through the broadcast.

gloss: The state of being tight — stiff, stretched, or short of room or money.
examples: He felt a *tightness* in his chest and called 911.
The *tightness* of the schedule left no room for error.
There's still some *tightness* in my hamstrings.

gloss: A sloping position, or the act of leaning something to one side.
examples: The picture hangs at a slight *tilt*.
A small *tilt* of her head told me she disagreed.
Give the pan a *tilt* so the butter spreads.

gloss: The particular quality of a sound that makes one voice or instrument different from another.
examples: Her voice has a warm, smoky *timbre*.
The two guitars differ mostly in *timbre*.
He can name an instrument by *timbre* alone.
contrast: Spelled like *timber* (wood) but said TAM-bur in American English.

gloss: A person or device that measures and records time, especially at a sporting event.
examples: The *timekeeper* stopped the clock with four seconds left.
Two official *timekeepers* sit at the scorer's table.
My phone is a better *timekeeper* than that old watch.

gloss: The measuring or recording of time, including hours worked.
examples: The company switched to an app for *timekeeping*.
Accurate *timekeeping* matters in a race this close.
Sloppy *timekeeping* cost several workers their overtime.

gloss: Lack of courage or confidence.
examples: His *timidity* in meetings held his career back.
The board was criticized for its *timidity*.
She got over her *timidity* by taking a speech class.

gloss: A medicine made by dissolving a substance in alcohol.
examples: She takes a *tincture* of echinacea all winter.
The shelf held a dozen herbal *tinctures*.
Put ten drops of the *tincture* under your tongue.

gloss: A place or situation that could burst into violence at any moment.
examples: The neighborhood has been a *tinderbox* since the shooting.
Dry brush turns these canyons into a *tinderbox* every August.
Both cities are *tinderboxes* right now.

gloss: Thin metal foil used to wrap or cover food.
examples: Cover the pan with *tinfoil* and bake it for an hour.
He wrapped the leftovers in *tinfoil*.
Wrap the potatoes in *tinfoil* before you grill them.
contrast: The package usually says *aluminum foil*; *tinfoil* is the everyday spoken word.

gloss: A ringing or buzzing in the ears that has no outside source.
examples: Years of loud concerts left him with *tinnitus*.
Her *tinnitus* is worst in a quiet room.
There's no cure for *tinnitus*, but background sound helps.
contrast: Two pronunciations are common in the US: TIN-uh-tuhs and tih-NY-tuhs.

gloss: Shiny strips of foil hung on a Christmas tree for decoration.
examples: The tree was covered in silver *tinsel*.
We were finding *tinsel* in the carpet until March.
She hates *tinsel* and puts up plain lights instead.

gloss: A long, angry speech of criticism.
examples: He launched into a *tirade* about the parking rules.
Her *tirade* went on for twenty minutes.
The coach's *tirades* are legendary around here.

gloss: An Italian dessert of coffee-soaked cake layered with sweetened cheese.
examples: We split a *tiramisu* after dinner.
Her *tiramisu* is better than the restaurant's.
There's *tiramisu* on the dessert menu tonight.

gloss: A person or company of enormous power or importance in some field.
examples: He was a *titan* of the steel industry.
Two *titans* of tech testified before the committee.
She's a *titan* in her field but shy in person.

gloss: A small gray songbird with a crest, common at American bird feeders.
examples: A tufted *titmouse* landed on the feeder.
Two *titmice* chased each other around the yard.
The *titmouse* takes one seed at a time.
contrast: The plural is *titmice*, like *mice*, though the bird has nothing to do with mice.

gloss: A lab method of measuring what a liquid contains by adding another liquid drop by drop.
examples: We did an acid-base *titration* in chemistry lab.
*Titration* gave us the exact concentration.
The doctor used slow *titration* to find the right dose.

gloss: A mushroom, especially a poisonous one.
examples: Don't touch the red *toadstool* by the fence.
*Toadstools* popped up all over the lawn after the rain.
The picture book had a fairy sitting on a *toadstool*.

gloss: A long flat sled with a curved front, used for sliding down snowy hills.
examples: They dragged the *toboggan* up the hill one more time.
Three kids fit on the *toboggan* at once.
He steered the *toboggan* straight into a snowbank.

gloss: The hard covering on the upper tip of a toe.
examples: He broke a *toenail* playing soccer.
She painted her *toenails* bright red.
An ingrown *toenail* can get infected fast.

gloss: A loose robe draped around the body, worn by citizens of ancient Rome.
examples: The statue shows a senator in a *toga*.
They wore bedsheet *togas* to the party.
His *toga* kept slipping off his shoulder.

gloss: A warm feeling of closeness among people who spend time with each other.
examples: The holidays are all about *togetherness*.
Sunday dinners gave the family a sense of *togetherness*.
He missed the *togetherness* of the old office.

gloss: A switch or control with two settings that you flip between.
examples: There's a *toggle* at the top of the settings page.
Flip the *toggle* to turn on dark mode.
The app has *toggles* for every kind of notification.

gloss: An item such as soap, shampoo, or toothpaste used for washing and grooming.
examples: Pack your *toiletries* in a clear plastic bag.
The hotel leaves free *toiletries* in the bathroom.
Shampoo was the one *toiletry* she forgot.
contrast: Almost always used in the plural: *toiletries*.

gloss: A small object used in place of money or a ticket, or something that stands as a sign of a feeling.
examples: The arcade still runs on *tokens*.
Please accept this as a *token* of our thanks.
Each subway *token* cost a dollar back then.

gloss: A small structure on a road or bridge where drivers pay a toll.
examples: We waited ten minutes at the *tollbooth*.
Most *tollbooths* on this highway are automated now.
Have your change ready before the *tollbooth*.

gloss: A light axe used as a tool and a weapon by some Native American peoples.
examples: The museum displays a stone *tomahawk*.
He learned to throw a *tomahawk* at summer camp.
Two *tomahawks* hung above the fireplace.

gloss: A small green fruit in a papery husk, used in Mexican sauces.
examples: Roast the *tomatillos* before you blend the salsa.
A *tomatillo* is firmer and tarter than a tomato.
The market had *tomatillos* for a dollar a pound.
contrast: The *ll* is Spanish, so it sounds like a faint y: tah-muh-TEE-oh, never *-til-oh*.

gloss: A girl who enjoys clothes and activities traditionally seen as boyish.
examples: She was a *tomboy* who lived in jeans and sneakers.
Both sisters were *tomboys* growing up.
He calls his daughter a *tomboy* with obvious pride.

gloss: A large, heavy book.
examples: He hauled a five-pound *tome* on Roman law to class.
The library keeps the oldest *tomes* behind glass.
Her biography is a nine-hundred-page *tome*.

gloss: The total weight or carrying capacity of cargo or ships, measured in tons.
examples: The port's *tonnage* fell for the third year running.
*Tonnage* through the canal is up sharply.
They charge by *tonnage*, not by the truckload.
contrast: The first vowel is the u of *ton*: TUHN-ij, not TAHN-ij.

gloss: The highest part or upper surface of something.
examples: There's dust on the *top* of the fridge.
We hiked to the *top* in two hours.
She wore a black *top* with jeans.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A hard clear mineral, often golden or blue, cut and used as a gemstone.
examples: Her ring holds a pale blue *topaz*.
*Topaz* is the birthstone for November.
The case held two *topazes* and an emerald.

gloss: The shape and surface features of the land in an area.
examples: The *topography* here makes farming difficult.
Rough *topography* slowed the search party down.
He studied the *topography* on the map before the hike.

gloss: Forward spin put on a ball so that it dips in the air and kicks forward off the bounce.
examples: She hits her forehand with heavy *topspin*.
*Topspin* is what keeps the ball inside the baseline.
Put a little *topspin* on the serve.

gloss: A state of being inactive and mentally dull, or a deep sleep-like state in animals.
examples: The afternoon heat put the whole town into a *torpor*.
Hummingbirds enter *torpor* on cold nights.
It took two cups of coffee to shake off the *torpor*.

gloss: A fast violent stream of water, or a heavy rush of anything.
examples: Rain came down in *torrents* all night.
The creek turned into a *torrent* after the storm.
She got a *torrent* of angry email about the column.

gloss: The twisting of an object caused by a force applied at one end.
examples: The axle failed under *torsion*.
*Torsion* bars replaced the springs on that model.
The vet operated for *torsion* of the stomach.

gloss: A wrongful act, other than breaking a contract, that a person can be sued over.
examples: The suit was filed as a *tort* claim.
*Tort* reform has been on the ballot twice.
First-year law students spend a whole semester on *torts*.
contrast: *Tort* (a legal wrong) sounds exactly like *torte* (a rich cake).

gloss: A rich dense cake made with ground nuts or very little flour.
examples: She brought a chocolate *torte* to the potluck.
The bakery makes three kinds of *tortes*.
One slice of that *torte* is plenty for two people.
contrast: Said the same as *tort*, the legal term.

gloss: Small ring-shaped pasta stuffed with cheese or meat.
examples: We had cheese *tortellini* in broth.
The *tortellini* only takes four minutes to cook.
He makes *tortellini* from scratch every Christmas.

gloss: The deliberate causing of severe pain, or something extremely unpleasant to sit through.
examples: The report documented the use of *torture*.
That three-hour meeting was pure *torture*.
He confessed under *torture* and later took it back.

gloss: A light throw, or the flipping of a coin to settle something.
examples: The game starts with a coin *toss*.
One quick *toss* and the keys were in my hand.
They settled the argument with a *toss*.

gloss: A flat fried tortilla served with beans, meat, and other toppings piled on top.
examples: I ordered two chicken *tostadas*.
The *tostada* fell apart when I picked it up.
She layers her *tostadas* with beans and avocado.

gloss: The whole of something taken together, or the period when a solar eclipse is complete.
examples: Judge the plan in its *totality*, not piece by piece.
*Totality* lasted almost four minutes in Dallas.
The *totality* of the evidence points one way.

gloss: An animal or object treated as the emblem of a family, clan, or group.
examples: The bear was the clan's *totem*.
Carved *totems* line the path to the museum.
That old truck became a kind of family *totem*.

gloss: The sense that lets you feel things through your skin, or physical contact itself.
examples: She could tell the fabric by *touch* alone.
The cat flinched at his *touch*.
Let's stay in *touch* after graduation.

gloss: A unit of local government smaller than a county in some US states.
examples: The *township* plows our road after every storm.
Three *townships* share one fire department.
He ran for *township* supervisor and lost by nine votes.

gloss: How poisonous something is, or how harmful a hostile atmosphere is.
examples: Tests showed high *toxicity* in the soil.
The drug's *toxicity* limits how much you can take.
She quit because of the *toxicity* in that office.

gloss: A small remaining sign that something was there.
examples: There was no *trace* of the missing hikers.
The lab found *traces* of lead in the water.
A *trace* of a smile crossed his face.

gloss: The work of following something back to its source or along its path.
examples: Contact *tracing* helped slow the outbreak.
*Tracing* the money took investigators two years.
The site makes *tracing* your family line pretty easy.

gloss: A device or program that follows the position or progress of something, or a person skilled at following trails.
examples: She wears a fitness *tracker* on her wrist.
The package has a GPS *tracker* taped inside.
The park hired an experienced *tracker* to help search.

gloss: A situation where you accept less of one good thing to get more of another.
examples: The lighter frame is a *tradeoff* for strength.
Every schedule involves *tradeoffs*.
There's a real *tradeoff* between speed and accuracy.
contrast: Often written with a hyphen, *trade-off*; both spellings are common in the US.
